steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our vision paper on GPU power capping at an academic supercomputing center as a way to make AI more sustainable. Cover the growing energy cost of training and deploying AI models, why existing efficiency techniques are not enough, and what we present and argue for.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. AI advances come at a cost: training large models
2. Deployment and AI infrastructure also use a lot of energy
3. Sustainability and existing efficiency techniques
4. Power capping as an alternative; what this paper presents

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Cost of training
- AI achievements: natural language generation, drug discovery, strategic games — not without cost
- training large NLP models: CO 2 comparable to lifetime emission of up to five cars
- hundreds of millions of parameters or more (GPT-4, Stable Diffusion); weeks to months of training on specialized hardware, petabytes of data
- widespread adoption: commercial use, non-traditional domains (information retrieval, drug discovery)
- trends continue -> more training data, compute, time, energy

2. Deployment and infrastructure
- deploying models also energy-heavy: GPT-3/4 behind ChatGPT and search engines, millions of daily users
- not only LLMs: object recognition, recommendation engines, autonomous driving, bio-informatics
- key players building new AI research supercomputing centers, massive compute and storage
- research ecosystem footprint beyond compute: conference travel, deadlines concentrated in warmer months

3. Sustainability
- systems grow in complexity/dimensionality and spread across domains
- impact on climate, energy sources and other resources as power and emissions grow
- trade-offs between performance, efficiency, sustainability = first-order question
- efficiency techniques: pruning, distillation, sparsification, quantization, data-centric (smaller representative datasets)
- but they reduce model/data size; need specialized knowledge or big changes to training/deployment

4. Power capping
- academic HPC and commercial cloud operators: limit power drawn by hardware
- vision paper: empirical observations + statistical analysis, 60% GPU power cap at academic supercomputing center
- lower GPU energy consumption at datacenter, lower operating temperatures
- argue for adoption: extend hardware lifetime, amortize embodied carbon, and more

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in what AI systems can do have led to stunning achievements, from realistic natural language generation to helping with drug discovery and winning complex, strategic games, but this does not come without cost. For example, training large-scale NLP models can emit CO 2 amounts comparable to the lifetime emission of up to five cars. Many of these models have hundreds of millions of parameters or even more (e.g., GPT-4, Stable Diffusion), and they sometimes need weeks to months of training on specialized hardware and petabytes of data to get such impressive performance. These large-scale models are also being adopted and applied widely, from commercial usage to non-traditional domains such as information retrieval and drug discovery. If the current trends continue, these models will need more and more resources in the form of training data, compute resources, time, and energy.

Training on large datasets is not the only problem, because deploying models can also use a lot of energy. Models like GPT-3/4 that power applications such as ChatGPT and existing search engines can be a huge source of energy use since millions of users use these tools every day. Large language models (LLMs) get a lot of attention right now, but a lot of resources are also used to train and run inference for machine/deep learning systems in other domains, with applications in object recognition, recommendation engines, autonomous driving, bio-informatics, etc. The race for further advances in AI has also led many large, key players to build new AI research supercomputing centers with massive amounts of compute and storage meant for ever larger computational workloads for AI research. The AI research ecosystem itself can also have a considerable carbon footprint outside of compute, for example travel (to/from conferences), conference deadlines being concentrated in warmer months, and more.

[Sustainability]
- systems grow in complexity and spread across domains -> climate, energy sources, other resources
- trade-offs performance/efficiency/sustainability = first-order question
- pruning, distillation, sparsification, quantization, data-centric approaches
- but these shrink model/data; specialized knowledge or big changes needed

[Power capping]
- HPC and cloud operators can limit hardware power
- vision paper: empirical observations, statistical analysis, 60% GPU cap at academic supercomputing center
- less GPU energy, lower temperatures
- argue for adoption: hardware lifetime, embodied carbon, more

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in what AI systems can do have led to stunning achievements, from realistic natural language generation to helping with drug discovery and winning complex, strategic games, but this does not come without cost. For example, training large-scale NLP models can emit CO 2 amounts comparable to the lifetime emission of up to five cars. Many of these models have hundreds of millions of parameters or even more (e.g., GPT-4, Stable Diffusion), and they sometimes need weeks to months of training on specialized hardware and petabytes of data to get such impressive performance. These large-scale models are also being adopted and applied widely, from commercial usage to non-traditional domains such as information retrieval and drug discovery. If the current trends continue, these models will need more and more resources in the form of training data, compute resources, time, and energy.

Training on large datasets is not the only problem, because deploying models can also use a lot of energy. Models like GPT-3/4 that power applications such as ChatGPT and existing search engines can be a huge source of energy use since millions of users use these tools every day. Large language models (LLMs) get a lot of attention right now, but a lot of resources are also used to train and run inference for machine/deep learning systems in other domains, with applications in object recognition, recommendation engines, autonomous driving, bio-informatics, etc. The race for further advances in AI has also led many large, key players to build new AI research supercomputing centers with massive amounts of compute and storage meant for ever larger computational workloads for AI research. The AI research ecosystem itself can also have a considerable carbon footprint outside of compute, for example travel (to/from conferences), conference deadlines being concentrated in warmer months, and more.

The core issue behind these intensive resource needs is sustainability. These systems will keep growing in complexity and dimensionality to reach more impressive milestones, and they will also spread and be adopted in more domains. These factors can have more and more impact on the climate and put stress on the sustainability of energy sources and other resources, as the power needs and carbon emissions of these systems grow. So finding ways to get optimal trade-offs between performance, efficiency, and sustainability is a question of first-order importance for the climate and for the sustainability of continued AI development. There has been a lot of progress on model efficiency with techniques like model pruning, model distillation, model sparsification, quantization, and data-centric approaches that make it possible to train models on smaller representative datasets. But many of these approaches mainly rely on making the model or data smaller, which can require specialized knowledge or big modifications to the training/deployment process.

One possible way for academic HPC and commercial cloud datacenter operators to reduce AI's energy consumption at scale is to use the ability to limit the power drawn by the hardware itself. In this vision paper, we present empirical observations and a statistical analysis of the effect of power capping GPUs at an academic supercomputing center where we deployed a 60% power cap on GPUs. We show that limiting the power used by GPUs across the datacenter can reduce GPU energy consumption at the datacenter and also reduce operating temperatures. We argue that power-capping should be adopted in data centers to help extend the lifetime of hardware, amortize the embodied carbon of data centers, and more.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in the capabilities of AI systems have delivered stunning achievements ranging from realistic natural language generation to facilitating drug discovery and winning complex, strategic games—but not without cost. For example, training large-scale NLP models can emit CO 2 amounts comparable to the lifetime emission of up to five cars [1]. Many of these models have hundreds of millions of parameters or even more (e.g., GPT-4, Stable Diffusion), sometimes requiring weeks to months [2,3,4,5] of training on specialized hardware and petabytes of data to realize such impressive performance. At the same time, these large-scale models are seeing widespread adoption and application, from commercial usage to non-traditional domains such as information retrieval and drug discovery. If current trends continue, these models will require ever-growing resources in the form of training data, compute resources, time, and energy.

Along with training on large datasets, deploying models can also require significant energy consumption. Models like GPT-3/4 that power applications such as ChatGPT and existing search engines can be a massive source of energy use, as millions of users use these tools daily. While large language models (LLMs) currently attract a lot of attention, considerable resources are also used to power training and inference of machine/deep learning systems in other domains, with applications in object recognition, recommendation engines, autonomous driving, bio-informatics, etc. The race towards further advances in AI has also spurred many large, key players to construct new AI research supercomputing centers [6] with massive amounts of compute and storage geared towards ever larger computational workloads for AI research. The AI research ecosystem itself can also induce a considerable carbon footprint aside from compute, in the form of travel (to/from conferences), concentration of conference deadlines in warmer months, and more [7].

At the core of these intensive resource needs is the issue of sustainability: these systems will not only continue to grow in complexity and dimensionality to achieve increasingly impressive milestones, but will also see increasing proliferation and adoption across various domains. These factors can increasingly impact the climate, stressing the sustainability of energy sources and other resources as the power needs and carbon emissions of these systems grow. Therefore, finding optimal trade-offs between performance, efficiency, and sustainability is a question of first-order importance for the climate and for the sustainability of continued AI development. Substantial progress has been made in improving model efficiency through techniques like model pruning [8], model distillation [9], model sparsification [10], quantization [11], and data-centric approaches that enable model training on smaller representative datasets [12]. However, many of these approaches rely primarily on reducing the size of the model or data, which can require specialized knowledge or significant modifications to the training/deployment process.

One potential path for academic HPC and commercial cloud datacenter operators to reduce AI's energy consumption at scale is to leverage the ability to limit the power drawn by the hardware itself. In this vision paper, we present empirical observations and a statistical analysis of the effect of power capping GPUs at an academic supercomputing center where we deployed a 60% power cap on GPUs. We show that limiting the power used by GPUs across the datacenter can reduce GPU energy consumption at the datacenter while also reducing operating temperatures. We argue that power-capping should be adopted in data centers to help extend the lifetime of hardware, amortize the embodied carbon of data centers, and more.
